analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress, the President, and senior officials from owning or trading individual stocks.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by a Democrat and co-sponsored by a Republican, never left the Senate committee it was referred to and received no vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would prohibit members of Congress, the President, the Vice President, and their spouses and dependent children from holding or trading individual stocks, bonds, commodities, and similar investments while in office and for six months after leaving. It would allow only diversified mutual funds, diversified ETFs, and Treasury securities. It would also apply the same ban to senior executive branch officials and top military officers, impose $500 fines for late or missing trade reports under the STOCK Act, require officials to disclose when they or their families apply for or receive federal contracts, loans, or grants, and create a searchable public online database of all financial disclosures.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, who would no longer see lawmakers and senior officials shaping policy while holding financial stakes in the companies those decisions affect. Diversified fund investors gain a modest benefit because officials' savings would flow only into broad-market funds rather than individual stock picks.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary citizens concerned about official conflicts of interest

how_it_helps.text: Members of Congress, the President, the Vice President, and their spouses and dependent children would be barred from holding, buying, or selling individual securities, commodities, or derivatives while in office and for 180 days after leaving, and would have to divest existing holdings within 180 days [S2].
The same ban would cover Senior Executive Service officials, general and flag officers (O-7 and above), and their spouses and dependent children [S2].

Exemptions would allow only diversified mutual funds, diversified ETFs, and U.S. Treasury securities, so officials could still save for retirement without holding positions in individual companies [S2].
Officials who violated the ban would have to forfeit any profits to the Treasury and face fines of at least 10 percent of the value of the traded interest [S2].
The bill would impose a $500 fine each time an official fails to file a required transaction report under the STOCK Act, closing a loophole where late disclosures carried no meaningful penalty [S2].
It would require disclosure within 30 days when covered officials or their families apply for or receive federal contracts, loans, or grants [S2].
Financial disclosure and transaction reports for members of Congress and senior executive officials would be posted online in a searchable, downloadable database accessible through an API [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress, senior executive officials, top military officers, and their families, who would have to divest individual holdings and could no longer trade them; the wealthiest officeholders with large individual stock portfolios would bear the largest cost. Securities brokerages would lose some trading business from this small group.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and senior officials with stock holdings

drawbacks.text: The ban reaches spouses and dependent children, which raises fairness and privacy concerns: a family's entire household savings would be constrained even though the spouse has an independent career [S2].

Enforcement depends heavily on the ethics offices themselves, and the bill's fines ($500 for a missed report; fines set by the Office of the Special Counsel) are modest relative to the wealth of the officials covered, so compliance would rely on disclosure and public scrutiny [S2].

A 180-day post-service trading ban could make it harder for departing senior officials to return to private-sector careers that commonly involve equity compensation, which critics of such bans argue may deter qualified people from serving [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is narrow but real: roughly 535 members of Congress, the President and Vice President, and a few thousand senior executives and generals would give up the ability to hold individual stocks in exchange for removing a direct conflict between their personal portfolios and their public decisions. The exemptions for diversified funds and Treasuries preserve normal retirement saving, so the cost to officials is convenience and upside, not basic financial security. The main weaknesses are enforcement design and the extension to family members, not the principle.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred the bill to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the bill on July 25, 2023, with Sen. Josh Hawley as co-sponsor [S1].
The Senate's only action was to read the bill twice and refer it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs [S4].
No further action appears in the record: the committee never reported the bill, the Senate never debated it, and no vote was ever taken [S4].
The bill carried over to no successor and expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress and senior executive officials who hold individual stocks are better off, since nothing now prevents them from trading securities while making the policy decisions those securities depend on. No ordinary person gained anything from the bill's death; its value to the public was the conflict-of-interest rules it would have created.

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban stock ownership by members of Congress, the President, and senior officials.

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Co-sponsored the bill, making it a bipartisan effort from introduction.

against.name: Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over government ethics legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no action; it never held a markup or voted, and the bill never reached the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from the start — a Democratic sponsor and a single Republican co-sponsor (1 of 49 Senate Republicans) — but with so few senators attached, the record shows no party-wide positions to measure; the outcome was determined in committee without a vote.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and senior executive branch officials
industries.note: These officeholders are the group the bill would have directly restricted, forcing them to divest individual stocks and end corporate board service. Their interest in continuing to trade individual securities while shaping policy runs against the public's interest in officials without personal financial conflicts.

industries.industry: Diversified mutual fund and ETF managers
industries.note: The bill's exemptions would route officials' investments exclusively into diversified mutual funds, diversified ETFs, and Treasuries, making these the only permitted vehicles. The effect is modest in dollar terms since it applies to a few thousand households.
Brokerages would lose the individual-stock trading and board-service relationship business of the covered officials. The loss is small relative to their overall volume.
